direction: Keep the refined scope of D001 and make the recency-decoupling explicit in the evaluation: the temporal layer is valid-time (as-of) gating applied post hoc across BM25, dense and hybrid retrievers; the benchmark is built by walking amendment chains so that a deliberately oversampled stratum of queries has a gold in-force version that is not the latest, with gold assigned by version identity and contamination measured per stratum. Report effects separately for the latest-gold and non-latest-gold strata, always including a recency-only baseline, and treat a null or small effect on the non-latest stratum as an informative negative result about when temporal re-ranking is unnecessary.
hypothesis: For time-specific queries over continuously amended regulatory text whose authoritative clause version is not the most recent, an explicit valid-time (as-of) temporal gating layer applied post hoc to standard retrievers reduces retrieval of superseded or not-yet-in-force near-duplicate clauses and improves answer accuracy relative to the same retriever with semantic similarity alone and relative to elapsed-time decay; on queries whose authoritative version is the latest, the temporal layer adds no benefit over a recency prior.
rationale: Evidence from three independent sources shows recency can be decoupled from correctness and that this is the condition under which the claim becomes identifiable: SituatedQA annotates the same question with different gold answers across temporal contexts; point-in-time financial QA is built on as-of dates and measures temporal evidence leakage, which presupposes past target dates; and legal identifiers encode entry-into-force and applicability dates, making the in-force version at a historical date derivable. The survey's warning about recency bias and the legal framework's bitemporal requirement show that a recency prior is not merely redundant but potentially wrong. This direction deserves investigation next because it converts a partially pre-empted method claim into a falsifiable measurement claim with a clear expected boundary condition (no benefit on the latest-gold stratum), and the main cost is benchmark construction rather than algorithmic novelty.
research_question: On queries over continuously amended regulatory text whose authoritative clause version is not the most recent, does valid-time (as-of) temporal gating applied post hoc to sparse, dense and hybrid retrievers reduce retrieval of superseded or not-yet-in-force near-duplicate clauses and improve answer accuracy, compared with semantic-only retrieval, elapsed-time decay, and a hard as-of filter - and does the benefit vanish on queries whose authoritative version is the latest?
